groups.title: Expanding
groups.blurb: Producing the multiplied-out form: distribute a factor, square a binomial. The active twin of the recognition skills.

skills.name: Expand: multiply into a bracket
skills.note: Produce the multiplied-out form: the outside factor lands on every term inside. $a(b+c) = ab + ac$. This is the active twin of recognising $2(x+1) = 2x+2$ — there you check equality, here you generate it — and the commonest slip is stopping after the first term ($a(b+c) \to ab + c$). A leading minus is the factor $-1$: $-(b+c) = -b - c$.

skills.name: Expand a squared binomial
skills.note: $(a+b)^2$ is $(a+b)(a+b)$, not $a^2 + b^2$. Expanding gives the cross term twice: $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$. Dropping the $2ab$ is the single most common error in school algebra — a power does not distribute over a sum, because it is built from multiplication, not addition.

groups.title: Factoring
groups.blurb: The reverse of expanding — pulling a shared factor back out front, or recognising a whole shape and writing it as a product.

skills.name: Factor out a common factor
skills.note: The reverse of expanding: pull the factor shared by every term out in front. $ab + ac = a(b+c)$. It only works when the factor is in every term — $ab + c$ has no common factor to pull. Check by multiplying back: $a(b+c) = ab + ac$.

skills.name: Factor a difference of squares
skills.note: Two squares with a minus between them factor into the two matching brackets: $a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b)$. It works because the mixed products cancel — expanding gives $a^2 - ab + ab - b^2$, and $-ab + ab$ is $0$ (th.difference-of-squares). Two things to hold on to: the SUM of squares does not factor this way at all, and the answer is not $(a-b)^2$ — squaring a difference leaves a middle term ($-2ab$), which the true factorisation has none of. Check by multiplying back.

skills.name: Factor a perfect square trinomial
skills.note: Three terms in the shape $a^2 + 2ab + b^2$ collapse into one square: $(a+b)^2$ (th.binomial-square, read right to left). The middle term is what identifies it — it must be exactly twice the product of the two roots, which is the term students drop when they expand and the term they must find when they factor. With a minus in the middle the same identity gives $(a-b)^2$ (th.square-of-difference). Check by expanding.

skills.name: Factor a quadratic
skills.note: For $x^2 + px + q$, find two numbers that MULTIPLY to $q$ and ADD to $p$; they are the numbers in the brackets. $x^2 + 5x + 6 = (x+2)(x+3)$ because $2 \cdot 3 = 6$ and $2 + 3 = 5$. The two conditions come straight from expanding: $(x+m)(x+n) = x^2 + (m+n)x + mn$ (ax.distributivity, then th.collect-like-terms), so the middle coefficient is a collected sum and the constant a product. Both conditions must hold — a pair that gives the right constant but the wrong middle term is not a factorisation. Not every quadratic factors over the rationals; check by multiplying back.

groups.title: Simplifying
groups.blurb: Collecting like terms, combining powers, cancelling a common factor to a shorter equal form.

skills.name: Collect like terms
skills.note: Add the coefficients of like terms; unlike terms stay apart. $3x + 2x = 5x$, but $3x + 2$ stays open — a term and a constant are not alike. This is the active twin of recognising that $2 + 3x$ does not collapse: there you judge which terms are alike, here you perform the merge.

skills.name: Simplify a product of powers
skills.note: Same base, so add the exponents: $x^a \cdot x^b = x^{a+b}$, not $x^{ab}$. A power counts factors, and multiplying two powers stacks their factors, so the counts add. The mirror slip — multiplying the exponents — is what $(x^a)^b = x^{ab}$ actually does, one step away.

skills.name: Cancel a common factor
skills.note: A factor shared by the whole numerator and the whole denominator cancels: $\frac{ak}{bk} = \frac{a}{b}$. What you cannot do is cancel against one term of a sum — $\frac{3x+2}{3} \ne x + 2$. Cancelling needs a factor of everything above and below, which is why you often factor first.

skills.name: Combine fractions into one
skills.note: Write a sum, difference, or quotient of fractions as a single fraction. Multiplying and dividing go straight across ($\frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ac}{bd}$, and dividing flips the divisor: $\frac{a/b}{c/d} = \frac{ad}{bc}$); adding and subtracting do not — they need a common denominator first, so $\frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ad+bc}{bd}$, never $\frac{a+c}{b+d}$. The straight-across reflex is the whole trap: right for a product, wrong for a sum, because the fraction bar is built from multiplication and not from addition.
